papers.abstract: JEPA-style latent world models let embodied agents plan toward new goals with model predictive control, but they are still too slow for real-life embodied control: sampling-based MPC repeats predictor inference tens of thousands of times per plan, and even on high-end GPUs one planning step can take tens of seconds. We observe substantial latent locality in this repeated-inference workload: the predictor maps close actions to close latents, and inside a quantized predictor this closeness takes a form that hardware can exploit, differential bit-level sparsity. Unlike an input stream, whose temporal similarity is given, a planner itself decides which candidates it evaluates together, so the planner can choose its own references and, with reference forest sampling, manufacture more sparsity: it couples the sampled action sequences of each group to a shared root, with competitive planning quality. We build the accelerator on the insights of the rich line of bit-level sparsity accelerators and design it and the planner tightly coupled as a single co-design: the planner increases sparsity and exposes structure for hardware scheduling, and the bit-exact hardware effectively uses the sparsity that the planner creates. On three JEPA world models, our co-design is 1.28-1.80x faster than a dense accelerator and uses 38-52% less energy, and it is 1.22-1.58x faster than prior bit-sparse design and uses 16-36% less energy, with the same area. To our knowledge, our planner is the first planner that manufactures differential bit-level sparsity across its candidates and exposes its structure for hardware scheduling, and our co-design is the first algorithm-hardware co-design for JEPA-style world-model planning.
authors: Wenbo Zhu, Paul Yi-Chia Chen, Yuanhan Li, Zishen Wan, Christopher Torng
bullets: JEPA world-model planning is slow because sampling-based MPC repeatedly runs predictor inference at large scale.
The method groups action sequences around shared reference roots, manufacturing latent similarity and hardware-exploitable differential sparsity.
A tightly coupled accelerator uses this sparsity and planner-exposed structure for efficient scheduling.
Across three JEPA world models, it achieves 1.28–1.80× speedup and 38–52% lower energy than a dense accelerator.
Compared with prior bit-sparse hardware at the same area, it achieves 1.22–1.58× speedup and 16–36% lower energy.

papers.abstract: Videos provide a rich source of physical interaction for learning robot behavior without action annotations, yet effective latent actions must capture not only local transitions but also how those transitions evolve over time. We introduce ReLAP, a latent-action pretraining framework that couples local transition learning with recurrent multi-step prediction in a frozen JEPA representation space. A shared inverse dynamics model infers compact continuous latent actions from adjacent observations, while a latent world model recurrently predicts the future JEPA features. Because each predicted feature becomes the context for the next transition, errors at later steps backpropagate through the rollout to earlier latent actions, encouraging temporally coherent dynamics beyond pairwise reconstruction. We transfer this representation to a vision-language model using two complementary objectives: latent distillation from the frozen inverse teacher and recurrent future-feature prediction through the frozen latent world model. The resulting policy is then adapted to robot demonstrations with action flow matching. At deployment, the explicit latent-action and world-model branches are removed, and the fine-tuned VLM predicts physical actions directly, reducing inference complexity. With only 11M pretraining samples and 1.06B trainable parameters, ReLAP achieves 97.9% on standard LIBERO and 70.0% over zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations. On the LARY latent-action benchmark, ReLAP ranks second in both mean regression error and mean classification accuracy among the compared methods. These results demonstrate that recurrent action-free latent action pretraining can learn compact, temporally structured, and transferable representations for downstream robot control.
authors: R. Gnana Praveen, Ali Rouzbayani, Zhiying Jiang, Bidhan Roy
bullets: Addresses the limitation of pairwise latent-action learning, which may miss how physical transitions evolve over time.
Uses a shared inverse dynamics model for compact latent actions and a recurrent latent world model for multi-step JEPA feature prediction.
Transfers the learned representation to a vision-language model through latent distillation and recurrent future-feature prediction, then adapts it with action flow matching.
At deployment, removes the auxiliary latent-action and world-model branches so the VLM directly predicts robot actions.
Achieves 97.9% on LIBERO, 70.0% on zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations, and ranks second on both LARY metrics among compared methods.

papers.abstract: Masked modeling is the dominant self-supervised paradigm for point-cloud videos. However, it leaks the information it is meant to predict, whether it reconstructs masked points as in MAE-style methods or predicts their latent features. Because point-cloud tokens are anchored at points sampled from each frame, querying a target at its own position reveals where its geometry has moved, in reconstruction and latent prediction alike. For latent predictors, random spatio-temporal masks introduce a further shortcut, as visible frames on both sides of each target allow interpolation rather than forecasting. The pretext task thus reduces to completion. Once the target positions are withheld, a masked latent predictor performs only slightly better than copying the last frame. To remove this leakage, we propose PointWM, a latent world model that turns completion into forecasting by predicting the features and geometry of future frames from strictly earlier context. Each target is queried only with its last-seen position and timestamp, while a latent action learned without annotations is meant to capture the part of the future that the past leaves undetermined. On HOI4D action segmentation with a P4Transformer backbone, PointWM improves F1@50 over training from scratch by 24.9 offline and 29.1 under strictly causal inference. These results show the promise of latent world models as a leakage-free pretraining paradigm for point-cloud videos.Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/InitalZ/PointWM.
authors: Zhuoyue Zhang, Jian Liu, Jihua Zhu, Ajmal Saeed Mian
bullets: Masked point-cloud video modeling can leak target motion through target positions and bidirectional temporal context.
PointWM converts completion into forecasting using only earlier frames, last-seen target positions, and timestamps.
An unsupervised latent action models future information not determined by the past.
On HOI4D action segmentation with a P4Transformer, it improves F1@50 by 24.9 offline and 29.1 with strictly causal inference versus training from scratch.
The method is evaluated for point-cloud video pretraining and its broader effectiveness beyond this setting is not established in the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of PointWM. Target branch. EMA copies of the tokenizer and encoder encode the full clip without gradients into target latents h (Latenth). Observation branch. The student encodes the same full clip into zf ; the latent-action modules read these features, which are regularized by LVIC. Context branch. With causal temporal masking retaining only the frames before a one-frame gap, the weight-shared student encodes these frames into zc. Queried with last-seen anchor coordinates, target timestamps, and a latent action at, the predictor outputs target latents ĥ (Latentp) and residual anchor displacements from the last-seen coordinates. The latent predictions are supervised by Llat (L1 to the stop-gradient h), and the anchor displacements by the Chamfer loss Lpos. Latent action modeling. An inverse dynamics model (IDM) qψ infers a posterior over at from the change between pooled frames of zf . The prior pω is conditioned only on the last context frame of zc and the horizon. The loss LKL couples them with one-sided stop-gradients, allowing the prior to limit what the posterior encodes while the posterior teaches the prior. Action switch. During training, the predictor receives the posterior sample, which is replaced by the prior mean for 30% of clips. When the future is unobserved, the switch selects the prior. Only the student tokenizer and encoder are fine-tuned downstream.

papers.selection_reason: Directly proposes a latent world model for point-cloud video forecasting with unsupervised latent actions.
papers.title: Latent World Modeling for Point-Cloud Video Pretraining
papers.tldr: PointWM enables leakage-free self-supervised pretraining for point-cloud videos by forecasting future geometry and features from past context rather than completing masked frames.

papers.abstract: World models that support planning, control, and interpretable reasoning require latent representations that genuinely encode action. Yet the large-scale video data from which such models are learned overwhelmingly lack action annotations. Latent-action models infer action-like variables from observation sequences, enabling action-aware learning from unlabeled videos or trajectories. A fundamental concern, however, remains: a latent that improves future prediction may simply encode the current state, episode progress, task identity, or other predictive shortcuts. Existing evaluation practices---reconstruction loss, rollout fidelity, action recovery, or downstream performance---cannot isolate this distinction. We introduce the Latent Action Support Ratio (LASR), a dimensionless metric that measures, under offline evaluation on held-out data, whether a learned latent provides predictive support for action-related targets beyond the current state and non-action alternatives. LASR provides two complementary summaries: GeoLASR captures typical support, while WorstLASR identifies the weakest case. We instantiate the LASR benchmark with recorded actions and corresponding physical state changes as targets, episode-held-out splits, one predictor type for all comparisons, and positive and negative controls. Experiments on recorded robot manipulation data and a matched multi-task panel demonstrate that LASR detects known action information, rejects representative non-action shortcuts, and enables graded comparisons among imperfect latent representations. We further use LASR to train and audit a lightweight residual adapter, obtaining descriptively better point estimates whose uncertainty is assessed with paired comparisons. LASR thus provides a principled offline protocol for measuring action-related predictive support in world-model latents.
authors: Yu Zhou, Changsong Lei, Yixiang Wei, Kairui Wen, Huankun Sheng, Ming Li, Yeying Fan, Yu-Hui Wen, Yong-Jin Liu
bullets: Addresses the lack of action annotations in large-scale video and the difficulty of validating latent-action representations.
Measures predictive support for action-related targets beyond current state and other non-action alternatives.
Reports typical support with GeoLASR and weakest-case support with WorstLASR.
Uses held-out offline evaluation, recorded actions and physical state changes, episode-held-out splits, common predictors, and positive/negative controls.
On robot manipulation and matched multi-task data, LASR detects action information, rejects shortcuts, compares imperfect latents, and audits a residual adapter.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a metric to evaluate action-grounded latents in world models, directly addressing latent action model evaluation.
papers.title: Beyond Prediction Gain: LASR as a Metric for Action-Grounded Latents in World Models
papers.tldr: LASR evaluates whether world-model latents encode genuine action-related information rather than merely predictive shortcuts such as state or task identity.

papers.abstract: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.
bullets: Addresses the poor cross-embodiment alignment caused by learning latent actions primarily from video reconstruction.
Uses language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and create soft neighborhood supervision.
Combines cross-embodiment alignment with robot action reconstruction to ground the shared latent space in control.
Enables unified training on human and robot videos without requiring paired data.
Scaling general human video reduces downstream robot action prediction error, while task-specific human video improves real-world task success.

papers.selection_reason: Latent action model aligning human and robot videos for embodied foundation model training; fits embodied learning and latent action topics.
papers.title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
papers.tldr: SALA aligns latent actions across human and robot videos using language-guided semantic supervision, enabling embodied foundation models to benefit from scaling both general and task-specific human video.

papers.abstract: Parameterized-action MDPs (PAMDPs) ask an agent to choose a discrete action together with continuous parameters whose meaning depends on that choice. Model-free PAMDP methods act fast but need many interactions; model-based methods are sample-efficient but plan at every decision, which makes them slow to act. We introduce HyLI (Hybrid Latent Imagination), a model-based agent that learns a hybrid policy entirely in the latent imagination of a world model and acts with a single forward pass. To address learning problems that the PAMDP structure creates, HyLI adds counterfactual mode evaluation, which gives every discrete action a learning signal at every imagined state, and success-window replay, which keeps rare successes in training. On seven standard PAMDP benchmarks, HyLI is within one published standard deviation of, or above, the published score of the strongest model-free baseline in our comparison on all 7 tasks, reaches 90% of that score with 2.4x fewer environment steps than that baseline (5.0x when its reward-free pre-training is counted), and decides 67x faster than the model-based planner DLPA at its published planner settings. It is the only method in our comparison that is both more sample-efficient than that baseline and fast enough for real-time control.
authors: Atahan Cilan, \.Ihsan Mert Muhac{\i}ro\u{g}lu, \"Umit Can Bekar
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between fast but data-hungry model-free methods and slow model-based planners.
Learns a hybrid policy entirely through latent imagination in a learned world model.
Uses counterfactual mode evaluation to train every discrete action and success-window replay to preserve rare successes.
Across seven benchmarks, matches or exceeds the strongest compared model-free baseline’s published score on all tasks.
Reaches 90% of that baseline’s score with 2.4× fewer environment steps and decides 67× faster than the DLPA planner under its published settings.

papers.selection_reason: Model-based RL agent learning policies in latent imagination of a world model with latent action discovery, fitting world models and robot learning.

papers.abstract: Conditional generative modeling with limited target data can benefit from representations learned in a related source population. We develop a transfer learning framework for conditional flow matching that accommodates distinct source and target response distributions and dimensions. Two procedures exploit a representation learned from source data: TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head with the representation fixed, whereas TFM-Adapt jointly learns the head and a representation adaptation under a functional anchoring penalty. For explicit neural network classes, we establish bounds on conditional squared Wasserstein risk that account for source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch, and numerical integration. When the source representation admits a smooth correction, adaptation replaces the frozen mismatch contribution by the cost of learning the correction and a controllable regularization bias. An information lower bound identifies regimes in which adaptation attains a strictly faster conditional squared Wasserstein risk rate than any generator restricted to the frozen context information. We also develop independent validation procedure for selecting among fitted conditional generators. We show that the selection procedure satisfies an oracle inequality, and the switching rule guarantees, with high probability, no increase in conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator. Simulations and real data applications illustrate the gains from our proposed methods and the effectiveness of target validation in guarding against negative transfer.
bullets: Addresses conditional generative modeling when target data are scarce and source and target response spaces may differ.
TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head while keeping the source representation fixed; TFM-Adapt jointly learns the head and a regularized representation correction.
Derives conditional squared Wasserstein risk bounds covering source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch, and numerical integration.
Shows adaptation can achieve faster risk rates than generators limited to frozen context information when the source representation has a smooth correction.

A target-validation and switching procedure has an oracle guarantee and can avoid increasing conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator; simulations and real-data applications demonstrate practical gains.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a transfer learning framework for conditional flow matching, applicable to adaptation (test-time learning) and generative world models.
papers.title: Knowledge Transfer for Conditional Flow Matching: Frozen Estimation and Adaptation
papers.tldr: A theory-backed transfer-learning framework for conditional flow matching uses either a frozen source representation or an adapted one to improve generation with limited target data while guarding against negative transfer.

papers.abstract: Video world models promise general-purpose interactive simulators, but their training is limited by action supervision: action labels are scarce, fragmented across incompatible specifications, and do not scale with the unlabeled video pretraining corpus. A common workaround jointly trains an action encoder to compress consecutive frames into a latent action and a decoder to reconstruct the next frame from the previous frame and that latent, forcing the latent to capture only new information. This has two limitations: learning the action space from scratch can limit generalization to unseen domains, and the bottleneck trades expressiveness for separation, with tighter settings losing nuance and looser ones risking scene leakage under domain shifts. We argue for a different starting point: rather than learning actions from scratch, we start from a pretrained foundation model (V-JEPA 2), whose embeddings of a frame pair already carry substantial action information after large-scale, diverse video pretraining. The remaining challenge is to extract the action while discarding the scene. We propose a label-free contrastive adaptation framework that pulls together frame pairs sharing the same motion under a different scene and pushes apart pairs from the same scene with different motion, reshaping the geometry of the pretrained space without imposing a reconstruction bottleneck. We introduce a unified evaluation protocol along three axes (action expressiveness, scene invariance, and action-conditioned video generation quality) across robot manipulation, camera navigation, game, and driving benchmarks, most of which are unseen during adaptation. Compared with annotation-free latent-action methods, our representations are substantially more expressive while matching their scene invariance, and they yield world models that transfer demonstrated actions to new scenes more faithfully.
authors: Runjia Li, Minghao Chen, Junyu Xie, Philip Torr, Andrea Vedaldi, Tomas Jakab
bullets: Addresses scarce, fragmented action supervision in video world-model training.
Starts from V-JEPA 2 frame-pair embeddings instead of learning an action space from scratch.
Uses label-free contrastive adaptation: matches similar motion across scenes and separates different motion within a scene.
Evaluates action expressiveness, scene invariance, and action-conditioned generation across robotics, navigation, games, and driving.
Reports more expressive representations with comparable scene invariance and better transfer of actions to new scenes than annotation-free latent-action methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed learning pipeline. Left: Contrastive action adaptation. An anchor frame pair (ot, ot+k) is encoded as a two-frame clip by the OnlyAct encoder ϕθ, a pretrained foundation model with low-rank adapters whose weights are shared across all branches. The positive keeps the action but changes the scene: the moving region of the anchor, found by optical flow, is cut out and pasted at a shifted location onto the background of a different scene (for moving cameras, a different photometric augmentation of the anchor is used instead). The hard negative is drawn from a non-overlapping window (ot′ , ot′+k) of the same video, sharing the scene but corresponding to a different action. In the action space, the anchor is pulled towards its positive and pushed away from its hard negative. Right: Action-conditioned video world model. The frozen OnlyAct encoder ϕθ maps consecutive frame pairs into the learned action space, yielding an action stream α1:t that conditions an autoregressive video world model Gψ. Given past frames o1:t and the action stream, Gψ predicts the next frame ot+1, and is rolled out autoregressively to generate subsequent frames.

First, action transfer extracts an action stream from a demonstration video and uses it to condition the world model from a new initial frame, reproducing the demonstrated action with no labels. Second, real-action control learns a lightweight interface from real actions onto the learned latent-action space on a small action-labeled set, so that real actions drive the world model directly.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses the action supervision bottleneck in World Models by extracting action representations from a pretrained foundation model (V-JEPA 2) via label-free contrastive adaptation. This is highly relevant to Latent Action Models and Multimodal Foundation Models.
papers.title: OnlyAct: Extracting Action Representations from Foundation Models for World Models
papers.tldr: OnlyAct adapts pretrained video representations into expressive, scene-invariant latent actions for more transferable video world models without action labels.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human video (EHV) records close-range hand-object interaction (HOI) and the temporal structure of everyday activities, offering a potentially scalable source of experience for robot manipulation. Using this experience for robot control requires recovering useful supervision without recorded robot actions and accounting for differences in morphology, viewpoint, and action space. We define Ego2Robot learning as the process of learning or adapting robot manipulation policies from EHV, organized into four learning paradigms: explicit embodiment transfer, explicit action and task supervision, egocentric video representation pretraining, and latent action and dynamics modeling. The four paradigms differ in what they derive from human video: robot-format demonstrations, interpretable supervision, visual representations, or predictive models of actions and dynamics. For each paradigm, we trace what EHV information is extracted, how robot policies use it, and when the additional data is required. Besides, we review the benchmark datasets that cover EHV, robot demonstrations, and synthetic and simulated resources. This paper links EHV data's contribution to the task information preserved and the robot-specific grounding used during training or deployment. Finally, we identify challenges in physical feasibility, agent coordination, in-context adaptation, controlled evaluation, and predictive control.
authors: Yi Wang, Jingqiu Wu, Lei Yao, Zhaoshuo Li, Haoyu Zhu, Yirui Zhou, Huaiyuan Xu, Ying Zheng, Chuang Yang, Lap-Pui Chau
bullets: Organizes Ego2Robot learning into four paradigms: embodiment transfer, action/task supervision, representation pretraining, and latent action/dynamics modeling.
Analyzes what information each paradigm extracts from human video and how robots use it for policy learning.
Reviews benchmarks spanning egocentric videos, robot demonstrations, and synthetic or simulated resources.
Highlights open challenges in physical feasibility, human–robot coordination, in-context adaptation, evaluation, and predictive control.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses learning robot manipulation policies from egocentric human video, including latent action and dynamics modeling.
papers.title: From Egocentric Human Video to Robot Manipulation in the Era of Embodied Intelligence
papers.tldr: This paper surveys how egocentric human videos can provide scalable experience for learning robot manipulation policies despite differences between humans and robots.

papers.abstract: Protein engineering requires navigating rugged fitness landscapes, where small sequence changes can produce large functional differences, but experimental screening can only sample a small fraction of sequence space. Thus, a central challenge is to efficiently traverse the large combinatorial space of mutations in silico. We introduce ProTEUS, a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution. Pretrained on deep mutational scanning assays, ProTEUS learns a joint representation of sequence, evolutionary, and structural information using MutationFormer, a mutation-biased attention architecture. Variants are represented as states in this joint latent space, and mutations define actions whose functional consequences are predicted. To support exploration of many mutants, we developed a fast, physics-constrained all-atom predictor that utilizes explicit geometric constraint enforcement to achieve >10 fold increase in speed than AlphaFold3 with guaranteed physical validity. Lastly, ProTEUS refines its prediction and understanding of protein activity through closed loop experimental feedback to guide evolution toward a desired phenotype. ProTEUS surpasses established models in both zero-shot and supervised fine-tuning mutation prediction tasks. We experimentally demonstrate its utility in two closed-loop multi-objective engineering campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase, yielding variants with >10 fold higher activity than wild type. ProTEUS provides a world-model framework that connects virtual evaluation of mutational outcomes with experimental learning for efficient protein evolution.
authors: Yikun Zhang, Minghao Guo, Guangxue Xu, Peter Yichen Chen, Wojciech Matusik, Wengong Jin, Jingjing Chai, Kaiyi Jiang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of exploring vast, rugged protein fitness landscapes when experiments can test only a small fraction of variants.
Uses MutationFormer to jointly represent sequence, evolutionary, and structural information from deep mutational scanning data.
Models variants as latent-space states and mutations as actions with predicted functional consequences.
Includes a physics-constrained all-atom structure predictor reported as over 10× faster than AlphaFold3 while maintaining physical validity.
Outperformed established mutation-prediction models and produced variants with over 10× wild-type activity in two closed-loop campaigns on aldehyde dehydrogenase and levansucrase.
papers.selection_reason: ProTEUS is a mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution, using a physics-constrained predictor and feedback loops. This fits World Models (Latent Action Models, Interactive World Models).
papers.title: ProTEUS: A mutation-resolved world model for closed-loop protein evolution
papers.tldr: ProTEUS is a closed-loop protein evolution framework that predicts mutation effects, rapidly evaluates structures, and uses experimental feedback to guide engineering toward desired phenotypes.

papers.abstract: Learning control from action-free recordings is challenging because intervention effects are unobserved and policies may exploit errors in reconstructed dynamics. We present a hierarchical model-based reinforcement learning framework that uses shared structure across related systems to learn system-specific control policies from action-free recordings. A hierarchical dynamical system reconstruction model captures shared dynamics and individual variation through low-dimensional embeddings. These embeddings are then reused to parameterize shared policy and value networks, linking differences in reconstructed dynamics to differences in control. Policies are trained entirely via simulation under an explicit intervention model with additive latent perturbations. Piecewise-linear recurrent neural networks enable mechanistic analyses of the controlled dynamics, while decoder-based constraints make the immediate effects of interventions interpretable in observation space and permit interventions on one modality while protecting another from direct manipulation. On Lorenz-63 and double-pendulum systems, hierarchical policies improve transfer over independently trained policies. On Lorenz-63, they also achieve a higher mean reward than repeated planning with the same reconstructed models, perform comparably to methods trained with controlled interactions, and generalize to systems absent from policy training after embedding inference alone. Applications to neural-behavioral recordings demonstrate suppression of predicted movement under constrained neural perturbations. Together, these findings show how shared dynamical representations support transferable control and mechanistic hypothesis generation from action-free recordings.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of learning intervention effects when recordings contain no observed actions.
Reconstructs related dynamical systems with low-dimensional embeddings capturing shared structure and individual variation.
Reuses embeddings to parameterize shared policy and value networks, connecting inferred dynamics to control.
Uses simulated interventions, interpretable decoder constraints, and piecewise-linear recurrent networks for mechanistic analysis.
Improves transfer on Lorenz-63 and double-pendulum systems, and can generalize to unseen systems after embedding inference.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Framework overview. a: A hierarchical DSR model is trained on multiple related dynamical systems (“subjects”) and used as world model for MBRL. Subject-specific parameters φ(j) are obtained by projecting shared parameters Pφ onto low-dimensional subject embeddings S(j). These embeddings are reused to condition the policy πψ and value networks Qθ by modulating group-level parameters Pψ and Pθ. b: For unseen subjects, learning only a new embedding via DSR fine-tuning enables insertion into the control model. c: The high-dimensional dynamics are controlled only in the directions that are decoded (z̃t). To underactuate the problem and for application-specific constraints, actions are constrained to be orthogonal to the target modalities and target dimensions. d: In the Lorenz-63 benchmark, the actions only affect the y− and z−directions.

papers.selection_reason: Learns transferable control policies from action-free time series via dynamical embeddings and latent interventions, directly relevant to world models and latent action modeling.
papers.title: Learning Transferable Policies from Action-free Time Series Through Dynamical Embeddings
papers.tldr: A hierarchical model-based RL framework learns transferable control policies from action-free time series by embedding shared and system-specific dynamics, then simulating interventions to train policies.

papers.abstract: Recently, world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as a powerful framework for robot manipulation. By jointly modeling action generation and future observation prediction, WAMs can act and anticipate the outcomes of the actions. However, existing WAMs typically rely on frozen pretrained encoders trained with reconstruction, which may not produce representations well suited for robot control. In this paper, we tackle the problem of learning physicallygrounded, control-relevant representations for WAMs. We propose MDF++, a visuo-tactile world-action model that learns latent representations of multisensory observations end-to-end with a diffusion backbone. While naive joint training can lead to feature collapse, MDF++ introduces a multi-task learning strategy that leverages cross-modal correlations to learn task-relevant representations. We evaluate MDF++ on a suite of contact-rich manipulation tasks, including realworld bolt screwing and nut mating, and show that it outperforms WAMs built on frozen pretrained representations by up to 50%. Additional videos are available on our website: jointmdf.github.io.
authors: Zixuan Huang, Jinhao Yu, Zachary Charlick, Dmitry Berenson
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between reconstruction-trained frozen representations and representations needed for robot control.
Uses a diffusion-based visuo-tactile world-action model to jointly generate actions and predict future observations.
Introduces multi-task learning with cross-modal correlations to prevent feature collapse during end-to-end training.
Evaluated on contact-rich tasks, including real-world bolt screwing and nut mating.
Reports up to 50% improvement over WAMs using frozen pretrained representations.

papers.abstract: State-space models (SSMs) recover low-dimensional latent dynamics from high-dimensional observations, but latents are generally not identifiable from observational data alone. Interventional state-space models (iSSMs) use perturbations to break observational symmetries and identify parameters up to permutation, scaling, and shift. However, prior work restricts identifiability to linear latent dynamics and piecewise-linear emissions, excluding many behaviors characteristic of neural circuits. We extend iSSMs to a substantially broader model class: we prove that (i) affine identifiability holds under general injective emission functions and Gaussian latent transitions, and (ii) with interventions, identifiability up to permutation, scaling, and shift is preserved under general nonlinear latent dynamics. We validate our theory on simulated FitzHugh-Nagumo dynamics, and then demonstrate two applications: adjudicating between competing models of decision-making; and predicting responses to unseen micro-stimulation in macaque and human neural recordings, with proof-of-concept generalization to a held-out stimulation site in the latter. Finally, simulations yield practical guidance for designing stimulation protocols that improve identifiability.
bullets: Addresses the non-identifiability of latent states from observational data alone.
Proves affine identifiability with general injective emissions and Gaussian transitions.
Shows intervention-based identifiability up to permutation, scaling, and shift for general nonlinear latent dynamics.
Validates the theory on FitzHugh–Nagumo simulations and applies it to decision-making models and neural stimulation responses.
Provides simulation-based guidance for designing stimulation protocols that improve identifiability.

papers.abstract: We study whether \emph{long-horizon model-based value expansion} can serve as an effective framework in pixel-based offline reinforcement learning (RL). Long-horizon model-based value expansion from pixels is substantially harder than state-based environments, as the agent must learn both the representation and its dynamics, and errors from either can accumulate recursively over imagined trajectories. We introduce MAC-v2, which enables long-horizon model-based expansion from pixels by training a reconstruction-free latent world model with action chunking. By learning representations from prediction and control objectives, MAC-v2 does not need to encode control-irrelevant visual details that can hinder the dynamics prediction. Action chunking further mitigates the prediction error by reducing the number of recursive model predictions required for value expansion. Across diverse visual benchmarks including visual OGBench, MMBench2, Robomimic, and LIBERO-10, MAC-v2 achieves strong performance against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines. Our analyses show that long-horizon model-based value expansion is critical for the performance of MAC-v2, and that both action chunking and latent learning objectives are essential for reliable long-horizon latent imagination.
bullets: Addresses compounding representation and dynamics-prediction errors in imagined pixel-based trajectories.
Learns latent representations through prediction and control objectives rather than visual reconstruction.
Uses action chunking to reduce the number of recursive model predictions during value expansion.
Performs strongly across visual OGBench, MMBench2, Robomimic, and LIBERO-10 against model-free and model-based offline RL baselines.
Analyses indicate that long-horizon expansion, action chunking, and latent learning objectives are all important for reliable performance.

papers.abstract: JEPA-style world models learn action-conditioned latent dynamics without reconstructing observations, but distributional regularization alone does not ensure that their representations preserve information needed for control. We identify static collapse, a failure mode in which the encoder preserves episode-specific static content while suppressing manipulation-relevant state changes. Because static content is temporally predictable yet diverse across episodes, this failure can persist despite regularizers such as SIGReg. A controlled study on OGBench-Cube shows that introducing randomized backgrounds substantially degrades planning performance while leaving the underlying manipulation task unchanged. To address this problem, we propose motion-guided contrastive regularization. Our approach compares predicted latent transitions with transitions to candidate observations from the same episode, reducing the usefulness of static background identity for distinguishing action outcomes. Optical-flow similarities provide soft contrastive targets, allowing candidates with similar motion to receive similar supervision. Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, our objective encourages representations to preserve within-episode state distinctions and similarities between related transitions. Our method improves planning success over LeWorldModel (LeWM) from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube with randomized backgrounds and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, while maintaining comparable performance on four other visual-control benchmarks.
authors: Yiwen Chen, Qiqi Hou, Jisoo Jeong, Yinhao Zhu, Huaizu Jiang, Amir Said
bullets: JEPA-style latent dynamics can preserve episode-specific static content while discarding manipulation-relevant state changes, harming control.
Randomized backgrounds expose this failure: planning degrades even when the underlying manipulation task is unchanged.
The method contrasts predicted latent transitions with same-episode candidate observations, using optical-flow similarity as soft supervision.
Combined with latent prediction and SIGReg, it promotes within-episode state distinctions and motion-related similarities.
Planning success improves from 52% to 78% on OGBench-Cube and from 14% to 54% on LIBERO-Object, with comparable performance on four other benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Static collapse and our solution. (A) We train JEPA world models end-to-end on OGBench-Cube (Cube) and a variant with randomized backgrounds (Cube-RB). In Cube-RB, one background image is sampled per episode and held fixed throughout it. Only distant pixels (depth ≥ 1.0m) are replaced, so the robot, cube, and dynamics are unchanged and only task-irrelevant background variation is added. (B) t-SNE visualizations of the encoder embeddings, where each point is one input frame and each color one episode. On Cube-RB, LeWorldModel (LeWM; Maes et al., 2026) maps distinct states within each episode to tightly clustered latents, whereas our motionguided contrastive regularization preserves within-episode state variation. (C) Planning success of LeWM, Planning with Latent Dynamics Models (PLDM; Sobal et al., 2026), and our method. LeWM and our method perform similarly on Cube, but LeWM’s success drops on Cube-RB and is low on LIBERO-Object. Our method achieves the highest success of the three in all settings.

Figure 2: Motion-guided contrastive learning. The world model encodes the current observation xt and predicts ẑt+1. The true next observation xpos = xt+1 provides the positive sample, while other frames from the same episode provide negative candidates xm and xn. All observations share the same encoder. Image-space: Optical flow is computed from xt to each candidate. Comparing these fields with the positive flow assigns higher target similarity to candidates with similar motion (xm) than to those with different motion (xn). Latent-space: Angles illustrate cosine similarities between the predicted transition ẑt+1 − zt and candidate transitions zj − zt. Our motion-guided contrastive loss matches the resulting latent similarity distribution to the motion-derived target distribution through cross-entropy. The prediction loss aligns ẑt+1 with zpos. The grippers in the sample frames are highlighted for illustration purposes only.

Figure 3: Latent-space decoding on Cube, Cube-RB, and LIBERO-Object. Compared to LeWM, reconstructions from our frozen latents more clearly preserve the robot and manipulated objects on the challenging Cube-RB and LIBERO-Object datasets. Check our video demo for more comparisons.

papers.abstract: Robot imitation learning is limited by the scarcity of action-labeled data, while action-free demonstrations such as videos are abundant. Recent latent-action methods learn action-relevant representations from observation transitions, but they do not optimize latent actions for downstream control, leading to latent representations that are difficult for policies to model and difficult to accurately decode into continuous robot actions. This paper introduces ELA, an end-to-end framework for learning from video demonstrations via latent actions jointly optimized for policy learning and action decoding. ELA jointly trains a latent action model, latent action policy, and action decoder, enabling policies to leverage abundant video data with only a handful of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show that ELA consistently outperforms prior latent action baselines. Moreover, it integrates seamlessly with existing imitation learning methods through lightweight 4M-parameter action decoders, requiring no changes to policy architectures or training objectives. Additional materials can be found on: https://end2end-latent-action.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of action-labeled robot data by leveraging action-free video demonstrations.
Jointly trains a latent action model, latent action policy, and action decoder for downstream control.
Uses lightweight 4M-parameter action decoders without changing existing policy architectures or training objectives.
Outperforms prior latent-action baselines on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.
Scope: applies to imitation learning with video demonstrations and limited robot action labels.

papers.abstract: Surgical world models have the potential to provide intra-operative guidance, accelerate risk-free training and facilitate transfer of expert surgical maneuvers. However, the use of world models for transferring surgical expertise has been largely unexplored. Moreover, recent approaches in this domain have mainly relied on ground truth kinematics actions or expert annotations for specific tasks, limiting their applicability beyond the narrow range of tasks with ground-truth annotations. In contrast, existing works in the natural domain have shown promising results in learning latent actions solely from unlabeled videos and transferring the learned actions across contexts. We observe that this paradigm is short-sighted for the surgical domain, failing to capture the hierarchical and goal-directed structure of surgical procedures. Thus, we propose a novel multi-step action learning framework to learn context-invariant latent actions that are easily transferable across various surgical contexts. We perform extensive experiments on the publicly available datasets, SurgToolLoc-2022 and PitVis-2023, verifying our approach with both quantitative metrics and qualitative evaluation by surgical experts. We have published our code and the implementation details at https://github.com/bhattarailab/Surgical-Vision-World-Model.
authors: Saurabh Koju, Love Panta, Deepak Thapa, Rudra P. K. Poudel, Prajwal Ghimire, Angus Watson, Yash Raj Shrestha, Prashnna Kumar Gyawali, Binod Bhattarai

papers.abstract: Learning a universal action representation from video requires modeling dynamics that are consistent across different executions of the same action yet invariant to changes in embodiment and appearance. Existing latent action models infer actions from visual transitions, but their representations often entangle the underlying action with irrelevant visual variations, limiting transfer across embodiments. We introduce DreamX, which repurposes a pretrained video diffusion model as a universal latent action learner. Our approach extracts compact latent actions from the video model's rich spatiotemporal features, compressing each latent video frame by $\boldsymbol{300\times}$ ($\boldsymbol{1{,}200 \rightarrow 4}$ tokens). In addition, by leveraging the video model's generative prior, these latent actions capture action-relevant dynamics disentangled from visual appearance. The resulting latent space serves as a shared action interface across embodiments (human and robot), environments, and action parameterizations. On LARY-Bench, DreamX achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models. Moreover, actions encoded in one setting remain effective in another: the latent space supports any-to-any video transfer and zero-shot action transfer across diverse embodiments and environments. Furthermore, this shared interface also enables policy learning in a compact latent action space, reducing the computational cost of video-diffusion-based policies.
authors: Jisoo Kim, Chaehyun Kim, Junsu Kim, Jiho Park, Seongchan Kim, Eunbeen Hong, Soowon Son, Fu-En Yang, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses the challenge of disentangling action dynamics from embodiment- and appearance-specific visual variation.
Extracts latent actions from rich spatiotemporal video features and compresses each frame 300×, from 1,200 to 4 tokens.
Uses the diffusion model’s generative prior to create a shared action interface for humans and robots.
Supports any-to-any video transfer, zero-shot action transfer, and policy learning in a compact latent action space.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance among latent action models on LARY-Bench, according to the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 8: Query-to-video attention. We visualize attention maps from latent queries to video tokens during encoding. Across human and robot demonstrations, latent queries attend to dynamic regions, such as moving hands and grippers, capturing the underlying actions in each video.

A decoder initialized from the same pretrained backbone reconstructs future video from the latent actions and the initial frame, with auxiliary action supervision when labels are available. (b) Encoder and decoder attention masks control information flow among video, query, and action tokens. In the decoder, video and action tokens read the latent-action queries but do not attend to one another.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated body motion and hand interaction over time, and a plausible-looking command sequence can still drop a held object or leave an interaction incomplete. We present action-conditioned latent foresight, a latent world-action model (WAM) that evaluates proposed command sequences before execution. An action generator proposes joint motion-hand command sequences from vision, language, and the robot state. An action-conditioned endpoint predictor estimates the visual features each sequence prefix reaches and measures progress toward a demonstration-derived subgoal, while a joint temporal prior scores temporal consistency given the robot state and preceding commands. The robot executes the first commands of the best-scoring sequence and replans from the next observation. During training, action consistency regularization reconstructs the first demonstrated command from observed and predicted feature changes, encouraging the predictor to retain action-relevant information. On ten tasks in the humanoid loco-manipulation simulation benchmark SIMPLE, our method achieves 89.7% average success, compared with 73.7% for Psi-Zero and 82.0% for DiT4DiT. On seven real-robot tasks, it achieves 85.7% under standard conditions and 65.7% under unseen object configurations, while GR00T N1.7 achieves 70.0% and 48.6%, respectively. Project page: https://ju6276.github.io/Action-Grounded-Foresight/
authors: Ju Dong, Xinyu Xiao, Yiming Zhou, Tianshuo Yang, Xuerong Liu, Lei Zhang, Jian Chen, Haocheng Zhao, Yu Fu, Yujie Wei, Diwen Zheng, Alois Christian Knoll, Angela P. Schoellig, Ping Luo, Jianwei Zhang
bullets: Targets failures where plausible motions drop objects or leave interactions incomplete.
Uses a latent world-action model combining visual-language-state-conditioned action generation, endpoint prediction, and temporal consistency scoring.
Executes only the best sequence prefix, then replans from the next observation; training adds action-consistency regularization.
Achieves 89.7% average success in ten SIMPLE simulation tasks and 85.7% on seven real-robot tasks under standard conditions.
Performance drops to 65.7% on unseen object configurations, indicating reduced robustness to novel arrangements.

papers.abstract: Safe autonomous driving requires more than recognizing the current scene: the ego vehicle must anticipate how surrounding traffic participants will evolve under its own motion. However, existing end-to-end driving models typically encode scenes into dense visual or BEV features, leaving object-level interactions implicit. We propose (INTERACT INTERaction-aware Action-Conditioned Trajectory learning), a three-stage framework that learns a slot-based object-centric world model from unlabeled driving videos and transfers it to trajectory planning. INTERACT first learns recurrent slots that group dense visual features into temporally structured scene-entity representations without object annotations. It then infers latent ego actions from slot context and video transitions, and uses them to condition future slot prediction, capturing how ego motion and surrounding entities co-evolve. Finally, the learned slots, latent actions, and future slot predictions are distilled into a trajectory planner to guide trajectory generation and selection. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM and nuScenes validate the effectiveness of INTERACT. In particular, it achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM, with improvements in safety-critical collision metrics.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of predicting how surrounding traffic evolves in response to the ego vehicle’s motion.
Uses recurrent slots to discover temporally structured scene entities without object annotations.
Infers latent ego actions and conditions future slot prediction on those actions to model interaction dynamics.
Distills learned slots, actions, and future predictions into a trajectory planner.
Validated on NAVSIM and nuScenes, achieving state-of-the-art NAVSIM performance with improved collision-related metrics.

papers.abstract: Navigation world models predict future observations conditioned on navigation actions to support planning, but their generalization across real-world environments remains constrained by the limited coverage of action-labeled data. Action-free navigation videos provide diverse visual experience, yet lack the recorded actions required for action-conditioned training. We introduce OpenNWM, a generalist navigation world model with latent action pretraining. It learns universal latent actions from large-scale action-free videos through visual prediction pretraining, and further aligns them with physical motions via action-conditioned post-training. To support video pretraining, we curate NavAnywhere, a large-scale action-free navigation video dataset comprising 17.5 million visual observations from 15 heterogeneous sources. It captures navigation by ground robots, humans, and drones, with diverse viewpoints and motion patterns across five broad scene types: residential areas, public and commercial spaces, urban settings, parks, and natural landscapes. Experiments demonstrate improved visual prediction on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, together with improved navigation performance. These results show that latent-action pretraining enables diverse, action-free videos to improve dynamics learning and generalization for open-world navigation.
bullets: Addresses limited action-labeled data and poor cross-environment generalization in navigation world models.
Pretrains universal latent actions through visual prediction on action-free navigation videos.
Post-trains the latent actions with action-conditioned data to align them with physical motion.
Introduces NavAnywhere, a dataset of 17.5 million observations from 15 sources spanning varied agents, viewpoints, motions, and environments.
Reports improved visual prediction on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, as well as better navigation performance.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct observations of contact physics, local geometry, and interaction dynamics, making it a vital source of feedback for contact-rich manipulation. However, existing tactile manipulation studies are often developed and evaluated within specific task settings, making it difficult to systematically compare how tactile information contributes under different interaction conditions. In this work, we develop a benchmark in simulation comprising 128 tasks organized around three complementary evaluation regimes: Precise, Recognition, and Dynamic. The benchmark further includes controlled static and dynamic task variants and 12 perturbation settings for evaluating robustness under changes in visual and physical conditions. These settings motivate studying tactile information as a temporally evolving interaction representation rather than only as an instantaneous observation. We therefore propose an action-conditioned latent predictive world model that integrates tactile history and learns a tactile state through prediction of future tactile latents. Building on this representation, we design a model that conditions action generation on the learned tactile state and uses predicted future tactile information to refine candidate actions through predictive tactile reflection. Experiments on the proposed benchmark show consistent gains from incorporating tactile information across the evaluated regimes. Project Page: https://tacmind-bench.github.io/
bullets: Covers Precise, Recognition, and Dynamic evaluation regimes with static and dynamic variants.

Experiments show consistent gains from incorporating tactile information across the benchmark regimes.

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) learn latent variables from observations and use these to both predict the evolution of the scene and to generate actions. The prediction has to be of the whole scene, whereas only a portion of the scene causes actions. WAMs fitted to demonstrations do not, in general, guarantee that they will generate actions solely from the latent causes of the demonstrated actions (the action-relevant latent variables), as the model could just as well learn to imitate in this way whilst entangling the action-relevant latent variables with the nuisance variables. We therefore separate out what causes action from what prediction depends on. We prove that under a sparsity constraint the latent variables used to generate actions are an invertible function of the action-relevant latent variables alone and the true structure is identified up to a permutation of the latent variables. This requires neither sufficient temporal dependence nor any assumptions on how the unobserved regimes evolve and holds even when the action-relevant latent variables are statistically dependent on the rest. We therefore propose CWAM (Causal WAM), which incorporates the constraint into a pretrained WAM by adding a sparse routing path to its action head, with the world modeling objective remaining unchanged. Experiments on both synthetic data and real-world robots validate the theory as well as showcase the improved efficiency in closed-loop success.
authors: Juntao Cheng, Jinzhou Tang, Fan Feng, Henrik I. Christensen, Yujia Zheng
bullets: WAMs may entangle action-relevant factors with nuisance variables when learning from demonstrations.
A sparsity constraint separates variables needed for action generation from those needed for full-scene prediction.
Under this constraint, action latents are identifiable up to permutation, without requiring sufficient temporal dependence or independent latent factors.
CWAM adds a sparse routing path to a pretrained WAM’s action head while leaving world modeling unchanged.
Synthetic and real-robot experiments support the theory and show improved closed-loop success efficiency.

papers.selection_reason: Causal separation of action-relevant latents in world action models with robot validation; directly fits latent action and interactive world model interests.
papers.title: CausalWAM: Learning the Causes of Actions in World Action Models
papers.tldr: CausalWAM identifies and uses only the latent factors that cause demonstrated actions, improving closed-loop action efficiency without changing the world-modeling objective.

papers.abstract: Recent empirical and theoretical advances suggest that joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) may learn meaningful representations for action-conditioned prediction of future outcomes, thus becoming one of the foundational structures for world models. However, accurate prediction does not, in general, necessarily imply recovery of underlying causal states that give rise to the observed dynamics. This work investigates when and how JEPAs can recover the underlying causal states from observations. We first introduce a latent variable model, in which high-dimensional observations are generated from latent causal states whose dynamics are governed by action-conditioned transition mechanisms. Based on this formulation, we develop a general information-theoretic objective that combines conditional likelihood maximization for learning transition dynamics with entropy maximization for preserving latent state information. We then establish identifiability conditions under which representations learned by this general objective recover the underlying latent causal states up to component-wise invertible transformations and permutation. One key condition for such identifiability is sufficient action-induced variation in the transition mechanisms. Guided by this finding, we instantiate the general objective with an action-modulated Gaussian additive-noise model, yielding action-modulated JEPA (A-JEPA). Experiments on synthetic environments verify the theoretical findings under the identifiability conditions and robustness to moderate violations, while visual benchmarks demonstrate improved state recovery and transfer to unseen transition mechanisms.
bullets: Motivation: Accurate action-conditioned prediction does not necessarily reveal the causal states underlying observed dynamics.
Method: Formulates a latent causal-state model and combines conditional transition-likelihood maximization with entropy maximization to preserve state information.
Theory: Derives identifiability conditions allowing recovery of latent causal states up to component-wise invertible transformations and permutation.
Key condition: Actions must induce sufficient variation in the transition mechanisms.
Results: A-JEPA validates the theory in synthetic environments and improves state recovery and transfer to unseen transition mechanisms on visual benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Identifiability analysis of action-conditioned JEPA representations for causal state recovery; directly advances latent-action world models.
papers.title: I Act Therefore I Am: When Is JEPA's Action-Conditioning Enough to Learn Causal Mechanisms?
papers.tldr: The paper characterizes when action-conditioned JEPAs can recover causal latent states rather than merely predict future observations, and proposes A-JEPA to do so.

papers.abstract: We introduce Continuous-Action World Models (CoAWM), a framework for learning cross-embodiment spatiotemporal dynamics priors that support robot action generation across embodiments and execution frequencies. At its core is a shared latent function space that captures the spatial and temporal structure of robot actions. We learn this space through two stages. First, function pretraining brings trajectories from different embodiments and sampling frequencies into a common representation, learning shared dynamics priors through action reconstruction and consistency across temporal sampling views. By accommodating heterogeneous robot trajectories, this stage broadens the range of data sources available for pretraining and facilitates scaling to larger and more diverse datasets. Second, we connect the pretrained function space to a world-model backbone, enabling observations, language instructions, and the current robot state to condition the prediction of a latent action function. A single decoder takes any query time and returns the corresponding end-effector action. By separating shared dynamics priors from task-conditioned action selection and temporal sampling, our approach provides a unified foundation for transferring robot experience across embodiments and control frequencies.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring robot experience across heterogeneous embodiments and execution frequencies.
Pretrains a shared latent function space using action reconstruction and consistency across different temporal sampling views.
Connects this space to a world model conditioned on observations, language instructions, and the robot’s current state.
A single decoder produces end-effector actions for any queried time, separating shared dynamics from task-specific action selection and temporal sampling.
The abstract describes a unified transfer framework but reports no quantitative experimental results or explicit limitations.

papers.title: Continuous-Action World Models: Learning Cross-Embodiment Spatiotemporal Dynamics Priors

papers.abstract: Test-time compute mechanisms, such as retries, confidence-based escalation and non-local routing, are conventionally deployed as black-box additions to trained models. They typically add forward passes or halting heads, but give no structural account of what the extra compute buys or what it costs against the model's stability guarantees. We therefore propose a theoretical and empirical framework for test-time compute on a Latent Dynamics Model used as the memory. When an encoder's latent state $(q,p)$ is advanced by a damped symplectic (velocity-Verlet) step of a learned Hamiltonian, every mechanism that expands access has an exact phase-volume Jacobian, a bounded energy change and an exact latch-transport law. We split reachability failures into escape failures and reach failures. A Lorentz squeeze resolves escape failures by injecting bounded, re-absorbable energy. A gated canonical translation (a one-step channel across $C_T$) resolves reach failures at $\detJ=1$ exactly. We verify this certificate stack on a designed analytic testbed. Reaching just beyond $C_T$ with the squeeze requires energy that grows quadratically in the excess distance. The gated channel's energy cost equals the potential difference between its endpoints, which is zero on the matched channel measured here, and so does not grow with distance in this testbed. An untrained state-replacing map annihilates phase volume and erases stored charge, while the gated channel transports it. On a learned physics-structured memory, we show calibrated compute rationing and evaluate the scaling limits of non-local routing against a physics-free baseline. The main contribution is the formalization and verification of the certificate stack, not benchmark performance.
authors: Pratik Jawahar, Riccardo Maggioni, Jonas Petersen, Matteo Cozzi, Gian-Alessandro Lombardi, Marek Gajewski, Camilla Mazzoleni, Federico Martelli
bullets: Identifies two access failures: escape failures and reach failures.
Uses a Lorentz squeeze for bounded, re-absorbable energy injection in escape failures.
Uses a gated canonical translation that preserves phase volume exactly for reach failures.
Analytic tests show squeeze cost grows quadratically beyond the access boundary, while matched-channel translation has zero measured potential cost.
Demonstrates compute rationing and non-local routing limits on learned physics-structured memory; benchmark superiority is not the focus.

papers.selection_reason: Formalizes a theoretical framework for test-time compute on Latent Dynamics Models (physics-structured memory), providing certificates for stability and energy bounds. This bridges test-time learning and latent action models.
papers.title: Certified Access: Test-Time Compute on Conservative Physics-Structured AI Memory
papers.tldr: A physics-structured memory framework certifies test-time compute by controlling reachability, energy, phase volume, and stored-state transport.

papers.abstract: Time-series data play an important role in various tasks, such as weather forecasting, web traffic analysis, and speech recognition. Recently, pioneering studies have increasingly adopted Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) based encoders to learn time-series representations through latent-space prediction. However, they often overlook the underlying factors governing transitions between time-series observations. In this work, we hypothesize that explicitly modeling the information behind changes in time series can facilitate time-series modeling. Building on this hypothesis, we propose ACTS-WM, a self-supervised latent action-conditioned world model framework for time-series analysis. First, we introduce a latent action modeling approach that infers the underlying information behind time-series transitions as latent actions, without requiring explicit action annotations. We then develop a JEPA-based encoder and an action-conditioned world model to predict target time-series representations conditioned on the learned latent actions and task information. We evaluate ACTS-WM across 4 representative tasks on 22 datasets from diverse domains, covering univariate and multivariate forecasting and classification. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ACTS-WM can improve downstream performance over pretrained JEPA-based encoders by learning complementary representations.
authors: Chia-Han Kuo, Chengshuai Zhao, Huan Liu, Lo Pang-Yun Ting
bullets: Addresses the limitation of JEPA-based time-series encoders that overlook factors driving transitions between observations.
Infers latent actions self-supervised, without explicit action annotations.
Uses a JEPA encoder and action-conditioned world model to predict target representations using latent actions and task information.
Evaluated on 4 tasks and 22 datasets spanning univariate and multivariate forecasting and classification.
Reports improved downstream performance over pretrained JEPA-based encoders through complementary representations.

papers.abstract: On PushT, our fixed action updater (1,505 parameters) solves 8 of 16 scenes reserved from our configuration selection. The comparison planners perform as follows: Selected Adam (7 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 218.440s), adapted iCEM (2 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 49.309s), released LePlanner (16 tasks solved, total planning and encoding time 5.652s). The total planning and encoding time for our action updater is 59.079s. Note that our action updater does not satisfy the task-cost criterion we fixed before evaluation. We also conduct another matched experiment where we only replay the first ten commands in each context and then allow the next solve 4, 8 or 12 updates (subsequent solves all get 8 updates). Among all 16 contexts (8 scene clusters), the 3 budgets get 9, 8 and 7 successes, respectively. Interestingly, the extra updates did not rescue any failing task in this experiment. All the changes in success/failure happen in one scene cluster, where we observe that the extra updates decrease the costs of the selected latent world-model trajectories for our updater, while the tasks that used to be successes become failures. The code, weights, evaluators, execution traces and cost accounting accompany the paper.

In a matched replay experiment, allowing 4, 8, or 12 updates yields 9, 8, and 7 successes, respectively.
Extra updates lowered selected latent-trajectory costs in one scene cluster but turned prior successes into failures; the updater also did not meet the preregistered task-cost criterion.

papers.selection_reason: Learned planners and action updaters in latent world models; relevant to world-model planning.
papers.title: When More Planning Hurts: Learned Planners for World Models
papers.tldr: On PushT, a lightweight fixed action updater solves half the held-out scenes, while extra planning updates can reduce success rather than improve it.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) leverage large-scale vision-language pretraining for semantic robot control, but often lack explicit foresight into how robot actions change the scene. World-Action Models (WAMs) address this limitation by conditioning policies on predicted futures, yet existing approaches typically rely on computationally expensive video generation with substantial pixel-level redundancy. We present LaWAM, a Latent World Action Model that exposes predictive dynamics to robot policies through compact latent visual subgoals instead of reconstructed future video. At the core of LaWAM is a latent-action-conditioned Latent World Model (LaWM). We obtain LaWM by training a latent action model in the latent space of a pretrained vision foundation model and repurposing its forward decoder to predict future observation features for scene evolution. LaWAM then conditions action generation on these predicted latent visual subgoals to enable dynamics-aware robot control. LaWAM achieves state-of-the-art or competitive success rates (SRs) across LIBERO (98.6% SR), RoboTwin (91.22% SR), and real-world manipulation tasks while retaining low-latency inference. LaWAM runs in 187 ms per action-chunk prediction and achieves up to 24x lower wall-clock latency than pixel-space WAMs.

papers.abstract: Learning from experience is essential for building the next generation of agents that continually expand their capabilities. Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already internalize rich world knowledge, yet this knowledge is rarely leveraged to drive policy improvement through online interaction. Realizing this potential efficiently remains challenging, as policy updates shift the agent's interaction distribution, requiring the world model to adapt accordingly, while continually updating large pretrained models is computationally expensive. To address this challenge, we introduce Dwell, a model-based reinforcement learning (RL) framework that reframes a VLM as a recurrent latent transition operator, endowing it with the ability to predict, adjust, and act in latent space. Leveraging the VLM's own representations and its dual role as both world model and policy, the agent continually learns from real interactions to anticipate and evaluate action outcomes, and from latent imagination to improve its behavior. Across five interactive visual environments, Dwell achieves the strongest overall performance among trainable methods while substantially reducing the compute required for imagination, showing that effective world models for VLM agents need not reconstruct the future; they need to predict futures that are useful for action. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Tom111-lhx/Dwell
authors: Haoxi Li, Sikai Bai, Jianfei Ma, Qinglin Hou, Xiaocheng Lu, Tao Han, Jie Zhang, Song Guo

papers.abstract: Learning controllable world dynamics from heterogeneous interaction videos is challenging because robot embodiments use incompatible action spaces, while human videos lack native control labels. We present RynnWorld-Latent, a cross-embodiment video world model that uses the 3D-grounded latent actions introduced by RynnLAM as a shared conditioning interface. This representation enables joint pretraining on human interaction videos, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without requiring a common native action space. Built on a pretrained video transformer, RynnWorld-Latent combines global action tokens with an identity-initialized local pathway that aligns actions with future video latents. We pretrain on 23 datasets comprising approximately 553.5M frames and adapt the model to target robots through post-training. The framework supports two data-generation routes: digital teleoperation uses target robot commands to generate action-video demonstrations, while latent-action synthesis transfers source motion to an edited initial frame and pairs the resulting rollout with retargeted pseudo robot actions. Experiments show improved video prediction metrics on public benchmarks and two real-robot platforms, alongside qualitative action following when different action sequences share the same initial observation. Synthetic mid-training improves policy success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and both generation routes improve real-world policy success rates over real-demonstration-only training in the evaluated settings. These results support universal latent actions as a scalable interface for learning controllable visual dynamics across heterogeneous embodiments.
authors: Haoyu Zhao, Yinzhou Tang, Zixuan Wang, Minghao Zhu, Dongchi Huang, Xingyue Zhao, Qin Zhao, Kehan Li, Siteng Huang, Xin Li, Zhenyu Zeng, Mingxiu Chen, Deli Zhao, Zhongyu Li

papers.abstract: Direct-policy World Action Models (WAM) have demonstrated the benefits of decoupling action generation from explicit future visual prediction for efficient inference in autonomous driving and embodied control. However, they still require tens of denoising steps to achieve competitive action quality, incurring substantial latency and hindering real-time deployment. Simply reducing the number of denoising steps will collapse the nonlinear multi-step denoising trajectory into coarse updates, substantially degrading action quality. To reduce the denoising steps while enabling real-time action generation, we present an effective world action model with one-step action generation, namely OSWAM, for autonomous driving and embodied control. We argue that it is the absence of structured action priors in random noise initialization that forces direct-policy WAMs to recover coherent action sequences through iterative denoising. Hence, we construct imagination tokens to initialize the diffusion process, providing physical priors and action-conditioned representations. We further introduce privileged information distillation with future conditioning to enhance future-aware action generation. As a result, OSWAM can efficiently and effectively generate high quality actions in just one diffusion step. Our experiments demonstrate that OSWAM achieves comparable or even better results in both autonomous driving and embodied control than direct-policy WAM and Joint-WAM that require tens of steps. It obtains approximately $3\times$ speedup over direct-policy WAM baselines and supports real-time compiled inference with latency as low as 40ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. The project page is available at https://gwenzhang.github.io/OSWAM/
